concepts.def: Discipline developing functional manufactured objects, balancing form, ergonomics, materials and user experience.
Three-dimensional representation of a building at reduced scale, used to communicate spatial relationships and design intent.
Practice shaping the inside of buildings through spatial planning, surfaces, lighting and furniture.
Creation of physical environments for theatre, film and television, supporting narrative and character.
Discipline producing wearable adornment, ranging from precious metalwork to contemporary art pieces by makers like Wendy Ramshaw.
Practice making objects from clay fired at high temperature, encompassing functional pottery and sculptural ceramics.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Three-Dimensional Design — a core area of GCSE Art & Design.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Three-Dimensional Design brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Three-Dimensional Design.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which contemporary British ceramicist is known for the 'Vase of Tears' and Turner Prize win in 2003?
options: Edmund de Waal
Grayson Perry
Bernard Leach
Lucie Rie

mcqs.q: Which discipline focuses on shaping the inside of buildings?
options: Architecture
Interior design
Set design
Product design

mcqs.q: What can line in a composition imply, even without representing an object?
options: Only the outline of an object.
Just measurements.
A composition with no balance.
Movement, direction, emotion, and visual rhythm.
Visual equilibrium achieved with different elements of equal visual weight on each side.
The space between letters.
An unbalanced composition.
A composition with no balance.
